props.title: Rain of the Children
props.initialSlug: A father's quest to lift his Maori family's curse

sections.content: Vincent Ward's deeply personal documentary Rain of the Children weaves together Māori cultural history and personal tragedy through the story of Puhi, an elderly woman who was Ward's subject in an earlier 1978 documentary. The film brilliantly connects to other explorations of indigenous perspectives like Merata Mita's landmark Patu! (1983) and Barry Barclay's Ngati (1987), while employing techniques reminiscent of Werner Herzog's documentary approach in Little Dieter Needs to Fly (1997) - revisiting subjects years later to uncover deeper truths.

sections.content: Ward's signature visual style, developed in films like The Navigator: A Medieval Odyssey (1988) and Map of the Human Heart (1993), brings a dreamlike quality to historical recreation sequences. The director's personal involvement in the story - appearing on camera and narrating - creates an intimate meditation on memory, cultural displacement, and generational trauma that connects to other powerful New Zealand films exploring Māori identity like Once Were Warriors (1994) and Whale Rider (2002).

The documentary's innovative structure, blending archival footage, dramatic recreations, and contemporary interviews, establishes a complex dialogue between past and present. This approach recalls the work of other documentarians exploring cultural memory like Errol Morris in The Thin Blue Line (1988) and Sarah Polley in Stories We Tell (2012), while remaining distinctly rooted in New Zealand's specific historical context. sections.content: The film's exploration of Māori spiritual beliefs and mental illness demonstrates remarkable sensitivity, avoiding both cultural appropriation and reductive explanations. Ward's approach shows clear influence from his earlier experimental work like In Spring One Plants Alone (1981), while connecting to broader conversations about indigenous representation in cinema, as seen in films like Ten Canoes (2006) and Sweet Country (2017).
